Beatriz had already said no once, privately, in Felix's glass-walled office in Lisbon. A week later he asked again, this time with a deadline, and mentioned that people who "help out" tend to do well in reviews.

That night she sat at her kitchen table and drafted a message. She kept it plain: the two dates of the requests, what he had asked, her answers, and the file names of the reports involved. No adjectives. On Friday she sent it to the company's ethics line, with HR copied.

HR replied the same afternoon confirming receipt and offering a call on Monday. She read the reply three times, still nervous, but relieved that the matter now had a proper place to go.

qa.q: In which city did Beatriz work?
What was Beatriz feeling when she read HR's reply three times?
qa.a: Beatriz felt nervous but relieved, since the repeated reading shows she was checking that her report had truly been received.

qa.q: What could Beatriz do if the report seemed to go nowhere, and why?
qa.a: Beatriz could follow up in writing with the same dates and ask what happens next, because a documented follow-up keeps the process moving.

qa.q: How might Felix see the situation when the ethics line contacts him?
qa.a: Felix might feel surprised and defensive since his hints were made in private, and a written report now shows the pattern of requests.

grounding: When the manager repeats the request, the employee moves from private refusal to a factual written report to the ethics line and HR.

subtype: Approach: escalate to HR or the ethics channel if pressure continues [Revision]
passage:
The first time Ankita's manager asked her to backdate a loan document at the branch, she said no quietly, and he let it go. The second time, a week later, he said it in front of the cashier: 'Just do it. You're not the auditor.' The third time, on Friday, he left the file on her chair with a sticky note: 'By Monday.'
That weekend Ankita decided that private refusals weren't working. On Saturday she wrote to the bank's ethics helpline email. She kept it plain: three dates, the exact words of each request, the file number, and that she had refused each time. No adjectives, no guesses about why.
On Monday at ten, Sangeeta from regional HR called her. 'We've received your report. Thank you for writing it so clearly. The file has been moved to another officer, and we're reviewing it. You won't face any consequence for raising this. If anything changes in how you're treated, call me directly.'
Ankita put the sticky note in an envelope, in case they needed it.

qa.q: What did the sticky note say?
What was Ankita feeling when she found the file on her chair?
qa.a: Pressured and frustrated, seeing that private refusals were not stopping the requests.

qa.q: Why did it help to keep the report plain and factual?
qa.a: Dates, exact words and the file number made it easy for HR to act, without it becoming a matter of opinion.

qa.q: How does Sangeeta respond, and what might she be thinking?
qa.a: Sangeeta acts quickly and reassures Ankita, probably glad the clear report lets HR protect both the record and the employee.

grounding: Shows an employee moving from private refusals to a factual written report to the ethics helpline when a manager keeps repeating the request.

subtype: Approach: escalate to HR or the ethics channel if pressure continues [Revision]
passage:
Dear Amandeep,
You told me to write down what happened, so here it is, and here's what I did.
In October my team lead asked me to change the completion dates on three quality-check forms at the plant, so they would match the client's schedule. I said no the first time and offered to write an explanation instead. He dropped it. Then he asked again in November, twice, the second time saying my contract renewal 'depended on teamwork'.
That was when I stopped handling it alone. I reported it in writing to HR through the company's ethics portal: dates, his exact words, the form numbers, and my refusals. No opinions.
HR called me the next morning. They said the report was logged, that retaliation isn't allowed, and that the forms would be reviewed by the quality head. Since then someone else signs those forms, and my renewal letter came on time.
I was shaking when I pressed 'submit'. I'm glad I did.
Mehak

qa.q: How many quality-check forms did the team lead want changed?

qa.a: Frightened and shaking, but determined, and later glad to have done it.

qa.q: What made the escalation work well?
qa.a: Moving from private refusals to a written, factual report with dates, words and form numbers once the pressure continued.

qa.q: How might Amandeep feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Relieved and proud that Mehak followed the advice and was protected, and glad to have encouraged writing it down.

grounding: Shows an employee escalating from private refusal to a factual written report to HR when a team lead keeps pressing for false dates.
